content.title: About
content.content: Tea is an infusion made from the leaves, buds or flowers of the Camellia sinensis plant. Kombucha is a fermented beverage produced by the joint fermentation of tea, sugar and a symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast (SCOBY). Both products are popular for their taste and potential health benefits.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tea is the second most consumed beverage in the world after water.
There are more than 3,000 tea varieties, distinguished by processing methods.
Kombucha has been known in Asia for over 2,000 years and traditionally used as a tonic.
During fermentation kombucha produces a small amount of alcohol (usually less than 0.5 %).
The SCOBY looks like a jelly‑like “mushroom,” but it is not a fungus; it is a colony of bacteria and yeast.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tea, especially green tea, is rich in polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Kombucha contains probiotics that promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Improved hydration
items.content: Both drinks contribute to maintaining the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Blood sugar regulation
items.content: Some studies suggest tea polyphenols may improve insulin sensitivity.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: B‑vitamins and organic acids in kombucha may help strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: Black and green teas contain caffeine, which can cause anxiety or sleep disturbances in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Tea leaf allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to tea components.

items.title: Kombucha contamination
items.content: Improper fermentation can lead to growth of pathogenic microbes and higher alcohol content.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Kombucha’s low pH may irritate the stomach in people with gastritis.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Caffeine and certain tea compounds can amplify the effects of stimulants or anticoagulants.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steep tea in hot (not boiling) water for 2–5 minutes, depending on the type. Kombucha is usually consumed chilled; it can be diluted with water or flavored with fruit juices and spices. Both beverages are suitable for breakfast, snacks, or as a refreshing evening drink.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store tea in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place, protected from moisture and odors. Keep kombucha refrigerated in a sealed bottle for 1–2 weeks; discard it if mold or off‑flavors appear.
